How to tell what's yours to take care of

Reconnect You · Issue 21 · Daniel Lawson

A group member described her pattern like this. "I'm in a loop of hyper taking care of people. They don't even ask, but I jump into taking care of things."

No-one asked her. She was already moving. And by the time you're wondering whether something is yours, you're usually already doing it. Then two or three days later the thought comes. Hang on. Why is that mine?

The same woman said this about her caretaking: "This is what I can, this is what I know, this is what I'm very good at, and super good at. I'm really proud of that, to be honest. But it also makes me forget myself more and more." She's right to be proud of it. It's a lot of why people trust her, and giving it up would mean giving up being the one everybody comes to.

Whose outcome it is

How much they need you is the wrong question, because the answer to that one is usually yes. So you ask whose outcome this is, and who gets the benefit of it getting done. If the outcome belongs to them and you carry it anyway, you've taken away the thing they were about to figure out for themselves.

She put the question to herself in a session like this: "is this my part? Is this my responsibility right now? Do I now want to help and support? Or is it me going overboard with giving and supporting?"

She wanted a way to feel the moment while it's still happening.

The signal is small

Something doesn't sit right, and you let it blow over the way you've let it blow over before. Frustration, maybe disappointment, and it's small enough to carry. You've got a lot on, so you carry it.

Over time this can build into a more felt anger. Every emotion has a function. Anger's function is to be a catalyst for change. When it fires, you don't need courage anymore. You can set boundaries, stop tolerating things, end things, speak up. Suppress it and it becomes rage. It's like holding the ball under the water. Eventually you get tired, and when you let it go it shoots out really high.

Some of us were taught to suppress the anger as well. One participant said, "I never nurtured anger and rage. I don't have it." She also said, "I don't even realise my boundaries. Saying no. Everything." She'd gone looking for the anger once: "They told me to channel my anger and I looked inside and there was nothing there."

So somebody crosses the line and you let it go. You find out three days later, and by then there's nothing to do with it except resent it.

Two kinds of responsibility

Another already had a rule for this and shared it: "What is my business, what is yours, and what is God's. It's about what you get the benefits from. I get the benefits of promoting my offers because people work with me. But I don't get the benefits of somebody implementing my work."

She works with that framework and the guilt still fires.

Responsibility and caretaking look identical from the outside, and the difference is whose outcome it is. Responsibility is yours, their capability stays theirs, and you finish it and it's done. Caretaking is theirs, so they lean on you and don't grow, and three days later you're resentful and you can't say why.

Taking responsibility for what is not yours means you're set up to fail. You can't change them for them.

Caretaking is what runs in me. Taking care of something that isn't mine saves me from having to ask for anything myself. I said as much to someone on a call once: "that's a caretaking strategy that's protecting you from just asking the hard thing, because you're taking care of something that's not your responsibility to take care of." I was describing myself while I was saying it.

And there's another question many of us never ask. We ask, "what could I have done differently?", which anyone wired like this takes too far. The opposite question is what wasn't yours.

Compliance or a fight

Saying no feels enormous, because there are two settings and nothing in between. You absorb it, or you blow up. And since the second one damages people you love, the first wins every time and looks like maturity from the outside, and from the inside too.

A third put it like this: "It goes from compliance to fight." The only other option she could picture was blowing up at somebody, so compliance was never really a choice. That's often why capable people don't set boundaries. The setting they'd need doesn't exist yet, right?

The middle setting is smaller than the one you're imagining.

Expectations are the baby sister of boundaries. The subtle yeses, the small accommodations, the way people speak to you or expect things of you that don't sit right and that you let blow over.

Said early, as a preference, it stays a preference. Left to collect, it comes out later as drama, resentment, anger or frustration, and by then it does need the big conversation, which is the one you were avoiding in the first place.

Where to start this week

You use the body, because it's quicker than the thinking. So you catch the boundary while it's being crossed, through a physical signal, rather than three days afterwards.

A fourth described this as a muscle: "It's something that you flex that muscle constantly, like you do go to the gym." And the signal she listens for is specific: "when my body is saying, hey, I need to stand up for myself. Or, respectfully, no thank you."

She also said, "if I'm in action mode, I am not going to be able to hear any of the solutions." Which is why the rule has to be a question rather than a reflection. A question is small enough to ask while you're still going.

So, the two questions, while you're already three steps into it. Whose outcome is this? And who gets the benefit of me doing it?

If you've been the one everybody comes to for years, you already know how to take on a piece of work and finish it properly. What comes next is finding out which ones were yours in the first place, and the timing is the difficulty.

The signal that would mark the line either never got developed, or it comes days after the moment it was for. And you can't fix the timing from inside your head while you're already doing it. Someone else in the conversation sees it a few seconds before you do, and says so, and then it's in front of you while it's still happening rather than on Sunday.

And then it goes faster than you'd think. One of the women wrote down, in her last workbook, that she'd said no to a responsibility that was not aligned, and I told her no is the easy one when you don't have many boundaries. "I want this" is the next challenge, and it's the better one.

The Reconnected Man and The Reconnected Woman are our groups where we have these conversations together.
